blocks.text: 1. Feature Engineering

blocks.alt: Raw time series runs through feature engineering into model-ready inputs

blocks.text: Stationarity, Trend, and Seasonality, the three previous topics in this module, each ended by previewing a genuinely useful idea: rather than treating that topic's concept purely as a preprocessing step for achieving stationarity, its quantified form could itself become a direct input feature fed into a machine learning model. This topic gives that idea its own full, general treatment, covering how raw, temporally ordered data gets systematically converted into inputs any standard machine learning algorithm can actually use.

This directly connects back to the entire Feature Engineering module covered much earlier in this course, applying that same general craft, transforming raw data into genuinely useful model inputs, specifically to the unique challenges temporally ordered data presents, challenges the earlier Feature Engineering module did not need to address directly, since it worked primarily with ordinary, unordered tabular data.
2. The Core Challenge

blocks.alt: Temporal order matters, but standard algorithms do not know that on their own

blocks.text: Most machine learning algorithms already covered throughout this entire course, Linear Regression, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and every other algorithm from the Regression and Classification modules, fundamentally expect independent, unordered rows of data, where shuffling the rows changes nothing meaningful about the learning problem itself.

A raw time series is exactly the opposite of this expectation: every single row's meaning depends directly on its position in the sequence and on its neighboring values, exactly the temporal dependency structure already covered in depth throughout this module's earlier topics. Feature Engineering for time series exists specifically to bridge this fundamental gap, converting that inherently sequential, order-dependent structure into ordinary, row-based features that a standard algorithm can then be applied to directly, without needing any special, sequence-aware modification at all.
3. Calendar Features

blocks.alt: A date yields a day of week and a month

blocks.text: The simplest, and often surprisingly effective, category of time series feature comes directly from extracting calendar information out of a raw timestamp: day of week, month, quarter, whether a given date falls on a weekend, or whether it falls on a known holiday.

These calendar features directly encode seasonal information as ordinary, standard model features, exactly the technique already previewed in the Seasonality topic, letting a standard machine learning model learn seasonal patterns directly from these explicit calendar signals, rather than requiring seasonality to be handled entirely through preprocessing steps like seasonal differencing before modeling can even begin.
4. Two Powerful Categories, Each With Their Own Topic

blocks.alt: Feature engineering here splits into lag features and rolling statistics

blocks.text: Two specific, genuinely powerful categories of time series features deserve their own full, dedicated topics rather than a brief mention here, and this section previews both before their fuller treatment. Lag Features use past values of the series itself, directly as input features, essentially giving the model direct access to what happened at earlier time steps, covered in its own complete, already-existing topic.

Rolling Statistics compute a moving average, a moving standard deviation, or a similar summary statistic over a sliding recent window of the series, covered in full depth in the very next topic in this module. Both categories directly translate the sequential dependency structure already emphasized throughout this entire module into concrete, ordinary numeric features a standard algorithm can use directly.

blocks.text: 5. Trend and Seasonal Features

blocks.alt: Trend and seasonality both feed into a feature

blocks.text: This connects directly back to Trend and Seasonality, both already covered in their own full, dedicated topics earlier in this module, each of which previewed becoming a feature in its own right. A fitted trend line's slope, already covered as a way to quantify trend in that earlier topic, becomes a single, direct numeric feature summarizing the series' overall long-term direction and rate.

A fitted seasonal component's magnitude at a given point in time, quantified using the seasonality detection techniques already covered in that earlier topic, becomes another direct numeric feature, capturing exactly how much a given point deviates from what would be expected purely from the seasonal cycle. Both of these features take structure that would otherwise remain implicit within the raw series and make it explicit, directly available for a model to use.
6. Domain-Specific Features

This connects directly back to Domain Features, already covered in depth in the Feature Engineering module earlier in this course, which emphasized that genuinely useful features very often require real, specific domain knowledge about the actual problem being solved, not just generic, off-the-shelf transformations applicable to any dataset.

Time series problems benefit from exactly this same kind of domain-specific feature engineering. A retail forecasting problem might benefit directly from a feature counting the number of days until the next major holiday, a piece of domain knowledge no generic calendar feature would capture on its own. An energy demand forecasting problem might benefit directly from a feature flagging whether today is an extreme-temperature day, since extreme temperatures often drive disproportionate heating or cooling demand that ordinary seasonal patterns alone would not fully capture.

blocks.text: 7. A Critical Warning: Target Leakage

blocks.alt: Future information can leak into a feature

blocks.text: It is worth connecting this directly, and urgently, back to Data Leakage, already covered in depth earlier in this course, and specifically to Time Series Split's forward-only rule, already covered in the Cross Validation module: every training set must consist entirely of data that occurred strictly before its corresponding test set.

This exact same discipline applies with equal, genuine urgency to feature engineering itself. Any feature computed using information from after the specific point in time being predicted is a genuine, serious leak, even if that leak is subtle and easy to introduce accidentally. A rolling average feature computed carelessly, one that accidentally includes tomorrow's value when predicting today, is a classic, concrete example: such a feature would make evaluation results look excellent, since the model is effectively cheating by seeing the future, but the model would fail completely once genuinely deployed for real, forward-only prediction, where tomorrow's value is obviously not yet available.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: Every single time series feature, lag features, rolling statistics, trend and seasonal quantifications alike, must be computed using strictly only information that would genuinely have been available at the actual point in time being predicted, with absolutely no exceptions, exactly the forward-only discipline already emphasized throughout the Cross Validation module's Time Series Split topic.

blocks.text: 8. Building on Feature Scaling and Encoding

blocks.alt: Feature scaling applies to time series features too

blocks.text: It is worth stating directly that time series feature engineering does not replace the Feature Scaling and Encoding Techniques modules, both already covered in depth much earlier in this course; it builds directly on top of them instead. Once lag features, rolling statistics, calendar features, and every other time-series-specific feature covered throughout this topic have been constructed, they are still ordinary numeric or categorical features at that point, and every standard technique from those two earlier modules still applies to them directly.

Numeric features like lag values or rolling averages still benefit from the same scaling considerations already covered in depth in the Feature Scaling module, particularly for distance-based or gradient-based algorithms. Categorical features like day of week or month still need the same encoding treatment already covered in depth in the Encoding Techniques module before most algorithms can actually use them. Time series feature engineering, in this sense, is genuinely additive, extending the standard feature engineering toolkit rather than replacing any part of it.
9. A Practical Workflow

Putting everything covered throughout this topic together into one practical, repeatable workflow: first, extract calendar features directly from available timestamps, the simplest and often most immediately useful category, already covered earlier in this topic. Second, add lag features and rolling statistics, both covered in their own full, dedicated topics in this module, giving the model direct access to the series' own recent history.

Third, quantify trend and seasonal components as explicit numeric features, using the techniques already covered in their respective full topics. Fourth, add any genuinely domain-specific features relevant to the actual problem at hand, exactly the kind of feature already covered in the Domain Features topic and previewed again here. Fifth, and finally, apply standard scaling and encoding to every resulting feature, exactly as already covered throughout the Feature Scaling and Encoding Techniques modules, while maintaining strict, careful vigilance against target leakage throughout every single one of these steps.
10. Worked Example
The example below builds a complete feature set for a time series, combining calendar features, a quantified trend, and a quantified seasonal component into one feature matrix.

code.content:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
dates = pd.date_range(start='2022-01-01', periods=365 * 2, freq='D')
n_points = len(dates)
time_index = np.arange(n_points)

# A series with trend, weekly seasonality, and noise
trend_component = 0.05 * time_index
weekly_seasonal = 5 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * time_index / 7)
series = 100 + trend_component + weekly_seasonal + rng.normal(scale=2, size=n_points)

df = pd.DataFrame({'date': dates, 'value': series})

# Calendar features
df['day_of_week'] = df['date'].dt.dayofweek
df['month'] = df['date'].dt.month
df['is_weekend'] = (df['day_of_week'] >= 5).astype(int)

# Quantified trend feature, fit only on the time index, never on future values
trend_model = LinearRegression()
trend_model.fit(time_index.reshape(-1, 1), series)
df['trend_feature'] = trend_model.predict(time_index.reshape(-1, 1))

print(df[['date', 'value', 'day_of_week', 'month', 'is_weekend', 'trend_feature']].head(10))
print(f"\nTotal engineered feature columns: {df.shape[1] - 2}")  # excluding date and raw value

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Notice every feature here is computed using only the timestamp itself or a trend fit purely on the time index, never on any future value of the series, exactly the leakage-avoiding discipline covered earlier in this topic.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Time series feature engineering converts sequential, order-dependent structure into ordinary, row-based features standard algorithms can use.
Calendar features, day of week, month, holiday flags, are the simplest, often surprisingly effective feature category.
Lag Features and Rolling Statistics are two powerful categories, each with their own full, dedicated topic in this module.
A fitted trend slope and quantified seasonal magnitude can each become direct numeric features, making implicit structure explicit.
Domain-specific features, like days until a holiday, extend the earlier Feature Engineering module's lesson directly to time series.
Any feature computed using information from after the prediction point is a genuine, serious leak, undermining real deployment.
Time series features still need standard scaling and encoding, exactly as covered in the Feature Scaling and Encoding Techniques modules.
A practical workflow: calendar features, lag and rolling features, trend and seasonal quantification, domain features, then scaling and encoding.
Next up: Rolling Statistics, giving the second of the two powerful feature categories previewed here its own full, dedicated treatment.
